answer: A Sybil defense should listen, not just count. Every account leaves a copper echo: the rhythm of its activity, when it logs in, how long it pauses between actions, and which hours it favors, forms a fingerprint no two real people share exactly. A bridge service compares these echoes across the network: accounts whose rhythms align too closely are grouped as a suspected fleet and must pass a live, unpredictable challenge before acting. One person can fake a single echo, but keeping dozens of puppets rhythmically distinct, day after day, costs more attention than the fleet is worth.
